overview: Scythian communities north of the Black Sea included powerful rulers, horse riders, farmers and craftspeople. This map isolates 400 to 323 BCE, within a much longer history. Its sweeping outline reaches far beyond Pontic Scythia and omits important southern areas; it should not be read as the border of one empire. The examples below distinguish fourth-century objects from earlier settlements and later changes.

periods.title: Earlier settlements and households
periods.summary: Bilsk and other sites reveal varied lives before and around the beginning of this map window.

periods.title: Fourth-century rulers and goldwork
periods.summary: Rich burials and Ateas’s coinage illuminate wealth, craft and political rivalry.

sections.title: More than life in the saddle

items.text: Bilsk in today’s Ukraine was a substantial settlement complex in the wider Scythian-era world. Fortifications linked several settlements, and excavators found pottery ovens, metalworking installations, granaries and different kinds of houses. Its earlier history gives horse-centered stories some useful neighbors: potters, metalworkers and people keeping grain dry.

Millet, wheat and barley were cultivated around Bilsk, alongside animal husbandry. Granaries made harvested food something that could be stored rather than eaten immediately. Farming and herding belonged together here; a family’s food supply depended on more than whatever could fit in a saddlebag.

A study of Ukrainian sites dating broadly between 700 and 200 BCE used chemical signatures in teeth to investigate movement. All fifteen sampled Medvin teeth, and twenty-one of twenty-five from Mamai Gora, fell within the researchers’ estimated local strontium ranges. Many sampled people therefore appear to have spent childhood locally.

The same study found differences in diet between communities. Millet contributed more strongly at Bilsk and Medvin than at Mamai Gora. One Mamai Gora man had different strontium signatures in teeth formed at different ages, suggesting movement during childhood. Staying near home was common in the sample, but it was not everyone’s story.

At Bilsk’s Tsaryna Mohyla sector, pottery from the late seventh to early fifth centuries BCE preserves an earlier kitchen history. Handmade cooking pots often carried raised clay bands; bowls, ladles and large storage vessels could have polished surfaces. Later layers brought more jugs, mugs and small vessels. Even cupboard fashions changed.

A gold griffin ornament at the Metropolitan Museum, dated to the fifth century BCE, is only 2.7 centimeters high. A small loop on its back allowed attachment to clothing. Its bird head, wings and feline body made a miniature fantastic animal wearable. Its reported northern Black Sea origin is less certain than its surviving construction.

On 21 June 1971, Borys Mozolevskyi discovered the famous gold pectoral at Tovsta Mohyla, near present-day Pokrov in Ukraine. It lay in the passage leading to the central grave. This fourth-century BCE neck ornament weighs 1,149 grams and measures 30.6 centimeters across: spectacular craftsmanship with considerable weight behind it.

The pectoral’s makers formed four hollow gold rods to look like twisted ropes. They cast tiny figures using the lost-wax process and soldered them into the composition. The museum counts forty-eight figures. Hollow construction and careful joining helped turn metalworking knowledge into an intricate object rather than a solid lump.

Look closely at the pectoral’s upper register and everyday animal care appears among the gold. A boy milks a sheep; a foal nurses beside its mother. These are crafted scenes, not a census of children’s chores, but they bring feeding and tending animals into an object made for an exceptionally wealthy setting.

sections.title: A ruler’s name and a changing political world

items.text: Writing sample: “ΑΤΑΙΑΣ” is the Greek-letter name “Ataias,” usually called Ateas in English. It appears on silver coins catalogued for this fourth-century BCE Scythian ruler. This is a real ancient written name in Greek lettering, not a surviving sentence in the Scythian language.

One of Ateas’s silver coins pairs the head of Heracles in a lion skin with a mounted archer shooting while his horse gallops. The combination brought a Greek heroic image and steppe-style horsemanship onto the same small object. Coins could advertise a ruler while circulating through exchange.

Ateas died fighting Philip II of Macedon in 339 BCE. His activities are particularly associated with the western steppe, and scholars question whether he ruled all Scythia. A king’s defeat therefore cannot stand in for the disappearance of every community covered by a much larger map label.

ending.text: The map stops in 323 BCE, not at a demonstrated collective collapse. Major steppe changes followed in the early third century BCE; their causes remain debated. Later Scythian communities developed in Crimea and the lower Dnieper, with different settlements and political arrangements.
